definition: A society that has surrendered its culture to technology — not merely a society that uses technology (tool-using culture) or one shaped by it (technocracy), but one in which technology has become the totalizing framework for all forms of thought, rendering traditional sources of meaning (religion, art, family, politics) subordinate to technical efficiency; Postman argues America became the first technopoly
synonyms: the surrender of culture to technology
connective_patterns: technopoly as the surrender of culture to technology
the progression from tool-using to technocracy to technopoly
in technopoly, technology is both friend and enemy

term: amusing ourselves to death/娱乐至死
definition: The thesis that television has transformed all public discourse — news, politics, religion, education — into entertainment, not by censorship or state violence (Orwell's fear) but by making amusement the natural format for all experience (Huxley's fear); the danger is not that we are oppressed but that we are diverted, not that truth is hidden but that it is drowned in a sea of irrelevance
connective_patterns: Huxley was right, not Orwell
entertainment as the natural format for all experience
public discourse degraded by the imperative of amusement

term: medium is the metaphor/媒介即隐喻
definition: Postman's revision of McLuhan's 'the medium is the message' — the medium does not merely transmit content but constitutes a metaphor that organizes and transforms how we think; our media are our metaphors and our metaphors create the content of our culture, so that the shift from print to television represents not just a change in delivery but a revolution in the epistemology of public discourse
connective_patterns: our media are our metaphors, our metaphors create our culture
the great media-metaphor shift from print to television
the medium is not just the message but the metaphor

definition: The relationship between a piece of information and the action a recipient can reasonably take upon learning it — in oral and typographic cultures, information derives importance from the possibilities of action it enables (high ratio); the telegraph and television destroyed this ratio by flooding people with decontextualized information about distant events they cannot influence, creating a sense of helpless pseudo-knowledge
connective_patterns: the telegraph destroyed the information-action ratio
high information-action ratio: knowing Adelaide has whooping cough
decontextualized information produces helplessness

definition: The world created by the telegraph and photography in which events pop into view for a moment, then vanish — a world of fragmented, decontextualized facts without coherence or consequence, like the children's game where objects appear and disappear without connection; this peek-a-boo world is entirely self-contained and endlessly entertaining, demanding nothing of its audience and permitting no meaningful response
connective_patterns: now this event, now that, pops into view then vanishes
the peek-a-boo world demands nothing and permits nothing
the peek-a-boo world created by telegraph and photography

definition: The mode of thought shaped by print culture — characterized by rational, sequential, propositional thinking that demands sustained attention, logical argumentation, and the capacity to evaluate truth-claims; print put forward a definition of intelligence that gave priority to the objective, rational use of the mind, creating a population accustomed to complex, extended discourse and the habits of critical judgment
connective_patterns: print created the typographic mind
the typographic mind demands rational, sequential thought
typographic America founded on rational discourse

definition: The condition in which all public discourse becomes a form of entertainment — Postman's thesis is not merely that television shows entertainment but that television has made entertainment the natural format for the representation of all experience, including news, politics, education, and religion; every subject is presented as entertaining, transforming citizens into an audience
connective_patterns: all subject matter presented as entertaining
show business as the meta-ideology of television
the transformation of citizens into audience

definition: The television phrase that signals a shift from one topic to another entirely unrelated one — 'now...this' is the verbal embodiment of the peek-a-boo world, a conjunction that functions as a disjunction, connecting stories about war, weather, celebrity, and famine into an undifferentiated flow where nothing follows from anything else and no emotional response to any event is sustained beyond the transition
connective_patterns: now this means everything previous was of no real significance
now this as the linguistic embodiment of decontextualized news
the conjunction that functions as disjunction

definition: The condition in which the quantity of available information vastly exceeds the individual's or society's capacity to process, evaluate, or act upon it — information glut does not produce a more informed citizenry but a more confused one, as the sheer volume of decontextualized data overwhelms the mechanisms (institutions, traditions, narratives) that once gave information meaning and direction
connective_patterns: information glut overwhelms the capacity for meaning
more information does not mean more understanding
information without context is noise

definition: The prophetic insight from Aldous Huxley's Brave New World that the greatest threat to freedom comes not from external oppression but from the population's addiction to amusement — people will come to love their oppression, to adore the technologies that undo their capacities to think; Postman argues this warning, not Orwell's, describes the actual trajectory of Western democracies under the regime of television and entertainment media
connective_patterns: Huxley not Orwell was the true prophet
people will come to love their oppression
the Huxleyan warning about entertainment as social control
